items.questionText: Write the number four thousand, two hundred and six using digits.
stepByStepSolution: Four thousand is 4000.
Two hundred is 200.
Six is 6.
Put them together: 4000 + 200 + 6 = 4206.
commonMisconceptions: Writing 4260 by mixing up the order of the digits.
Forgetting a placeholder zero, e.g. writing 426.
hints: Think about how many thousands, hundreds, tens and ones there are.
Line up the place value columns: Th H T O.

items.questionText: What is the value of the digit 7 in the number 7,438?
stepByStepSolution: Look at where the 7 is in the number 7,438.
It is in the thousands column.
So its value is 7 x 1000 = 7000.
commonMisconceptions: Saying the value is just 7 instead of 7000.
Confusing thousands column with hundreds column.
hints: Which column is the 7 sitting in?
Multiply the digit by the value of its column.

items.questionText: Order these numbers from smallest to largest: 3,102  1,999  3,120  999
stepByStepSolution: Compare the number of digits first — 999 has fewer digits, so it's smallest.
Compare the thousands digit of the rest: 1,999 has 1 thousand; 3,102 and 3,120 have 3 thousands.
Compare the hundreds/tens of 3,102 and 3,120: 102 is less than 120.
commonMisconceptions: Ordering by first digit only without checking place value fully.
Treating 999 as bigger because it 'looks like a lot of 9s'.
hints: Start by comparing how many digits each number has.
For numbers with the same number of digits, compare from the left-most column.

items.questionText: Which metric unit would you use to measure how heavy your school bag is: grams or kilograms?
stepByStepSolution: Think about how heavy a school bag usually is.
Grams are used for very light things, like a paperclip.
Kilograms are used for heavier things, like a bag full of books.
So kilograms is the better choice.
commonMisconceptions: Choosing grams because it 'sounds smaller and easier'.
Not connecting real-world weight to the right unit.
hints: Is a school bag light like a feather, or heavier?
Kilograms are for heavier everyday objects.

items.questionText: Would you measure the length of your pencil in millimetres, centimetres, or metres?
stepByStepSolution: A pencil is a small object, shorter than a metre.
Millimetres are for very tiny measurements.
Centimetres suit everyday small objects like a pencil.
So centimetres is the best choice.
commonMisconceptions: Choosing metres because it feels like the 'main' unit.
hints: Is your pencil closer in size to your finger or to a door?
Centimetres are used for everyday small objects.

items.questionText: A poster says 'Come to the School Fair — Saturday 10am!' with bright colours and a big smiley face. What is the purpose of this text?
items.answerKey: to persuade people to come to the fair
stepByStepSolution: Look at the words: 'Come to the School Fair'.
Look at the pictures: bright colours and a smiley face.
These features are designed to make people excited.
The purpose is to persuade people to attend.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking it's just to inform, without noticing the persuasive images.
Focusing only on the words and ignoring the visual features.
hints: Why might someone use bright colours and a smiley face?
Think about what the poster wants you to do.

items.questionText: Put these three sentences in the best order to start a recount: (A) Then we packed our lunches. (B) Last weekend, my family went to the beach. (C) First, we checked the weather.
stepByStepSolution: A recount usually starts by saying when and what happened — that's sentence B.
Next comes what happened first — sentence C ('First, we checked...').
Then comes what happened next — sentence A ('Then we packed...').
So the order is B, C, A.
commonMisconceptions: Starting with 'First' before introducing the event.
Ignoring the sequencing words like 'then' and 'first'.
hints: Look for the sentence that introduces the event.
Look for sequencing words like 'first' and 'then' to find the order.

items.questionText: Join these two sentences with 'but': 'I wanted to play outside.' 'It started raining.'
items.answerKey: I wanted to play outside, but it started raining.
stepByStepSolution: Look at the two ideas: wanting to play outside, and it raining.
These ideas contrast with each other.
Use 'but' to join them, with a comma before 'but'.
Result: I wanted to play outside, but it started raining.
commonMisconceptions: Using 'and' instead of 'but' even though the ideas contrast.
hints: Do the two ideas agree or contrast with each other?
Remember to put a comma just before 'but'.
